text: Harrow Foods devised a food-drying manufacturing process. Marlowe Textiles later employed a comparable method. The same parameters appear in an expired public patent filed years before Harrow's work. The patent described the heating cycles and moisture targets without restriction. No other aspect of the parties' conduct is recounted here.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods developed a curing line for edible films. Defendant Marlowe Textiles built its own line in 2011. Published handbooks give the identical formulation for the polymer blend and press settings used in that process. The handbooks were stocked in public technical collections. The record mentions no agreements between the firms.

Marlowe Textiles began extruding protein sheets in 2004. Harrow Foods had earlier used a similar manufacturing process. The method is described in a widely available textbook on food engineering, which sets out the extrusion temperatures and feed rates. The textbook circulated through public university libraries. Nothing in the summary speaks to employee movement.

Harrow Foods operated a sterilization manufacturing process for packaged meals. Marlowe Textiles adopted equivalent steps. Public standards bodies specify the very tolerances at issue for thermal dwell time and pressure in open documents. Those documents were downloadable from agency websites. The opinion does not discuss any protective measures by Harrow.

Defendant Marlowe Textiles manufactured woven wraps via a steeping process. Plaintiff Harrow Foods had a like process. Any library's trade literature sets out the process for the enzymatic bath and rinse sequence. The literature was on open shelves. The case file is silent on whether the firms met to talk business.

Harrow Foods created a coating manufacturing process for grain. Marlowe Textiles used the same approach in its plant outside Leeds. The design is documented in openly available datasheets from a components supplier, showing the spray nozzle array and cure oven profile. The datasheets required no login. No reference is made to confidentiality undertakings.

Marlowe Textiles produced dried fruit using a belt process. Harrow Foods had earlier developed a comparable manufacturing process. Government filings disclose the same specifications for belt speed and ambient humidity in public inspection records. The records were accessible to any requester. The narrative contains no mention of plaintiff's access controls.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods refined a fermentation manufacturing process. Defendant Marlowe Textiles ran vats with matching conditions. The information is compiled in a public industry catalog listing culture strains and timing for the batch method. The catalog was sold at trade counters. The court's summary avoids any claim of deception by either side.

Harrow Foods engineered a slicing manufacturing process for tubers in 1998. Marlowe Textiles installed similar equipment in 2002. The same parameters appear in an expired public patent covering blade angle and feed pressure. The patent had lapsed before either company's project. No testimony indicates the defendant hired away staff.

Defendant Marlowe Textiles assembled a freezing tunnel for meals. Plaintiff Harrow Foods had used a parallel manufacturing process. Published handbooks give the identical formulation of the brine spray and airflow rate used to set texture. The volumes sat in public reading rooms. The brief does not state that defendant knew the data was restricted.

Marlowe Textiles roasted nuts using a rotating drum method. Harrow Foods had a like manufacturing process from the late 1980s. The method is described in a widely available textbook on thermal food treatment, with the drum pitch and gas mix stated plainly. The book was in public bookshops. There is no account of documents carried over by any employee.

Harrow Foods built a bottling manufacturing process with ultraviolet stages. Marlowe Textiles copied the layout in 2015. Public standards bodies specify the very tolerances at issue for UV dose and line clearance in freely posted standards. The texts were open to the public. The record stays neutral on any noncompete between the parties.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods used a milling manufacturing process for starches. Defendant Marlowe Textiles adopted the same in its mill. Any library's trade literature sets out the process of roller gap and sifting pass count. The pamphlets were unsealed. The summary notes no reverse engineering of a sold product by defendant.

Marlowe Textiles cured hides through a tanning manufacturing process. Harrow Foods had earlier cured foods by a like route. The design is documented in openly available datasheets from an equipment maker, listing drum speed and liquor ratio. The files were not gated. No indication appears that plaintiff waived any restriction by contract.

Harrow Foods ran a dehydrating manufacturing process for herbs. Marlowe Textiles set up a mirrored line in 2009. Government filings disclose the same specifications for tray loading and exhaust temp in public dockets. The dockets were open for inspection by any member of the public. The opinion is quiet on defendant's development expense.

Ironwood Chemicals and Pinnacle Agritech were parties to a dispute over a customer list. The names and regional allocations of those buyers were printed in an expired public patent filed by a third firm. The patent described the same distribution channels without restriction. Pinnacle Agritech obtained the list from the patent record.

Pinnacle Agritech responded to Ironwood Chemicals' complaint by noting that published handbooks give the identical formulation of the customer list at issue. Those handbooks were available in open circulation before the alleged misappropriation. The district court recounted that the list matched the handbook entries page for page.

Ironwood Chemicals had compiled a customer list for its oil & gas division. A method describing the same client groupings is set out in a widely available textbook on petroleum distribution. Pinnacle Agritech cited that volume, which any retailer could purchase, as its source for the disputed records in the 1990s.

The customer list claimed by Ironwood Chemicals in its gaming subsidiary was also specified in materials from a public standards body. That body had published the very account categories and tier definitions without access limitation. Pinnacle Agritech retrieved the document from a public reading room in 2004.

Pinnacle Agritech asserted that any library's trade literature sets out the process Ironwood Chemicals used to assemble its customer list. The literature, shelved in municipal libraries, contained the identical segmentation. Ironwood Chemicals did not dispute the public availability of those particular volumes during the relevant period.

Ironwood Chemicals objected that Pinnacle Agritech reproduced its customer list. The design of that list was documented in openly available datasheets issued by an industry consortium in 2011. Those datasheets listed the same account codes and contact bands, and Pinnacle Agritech downloaded them from a public site.

In the late 1980s, Ironwood Chemicals circulated internally a customer list for solvents. Government filings disclose the same specifications of buyer classes that Pinnacle Agritech later used. The filings were part of public docket records, and the defendant obtained the schedule from a county archive without special permission.

Pinnacle Agritech entered the gaming market using a customer list. The information is compiled in a public industry catalog that predates Ironwood Chemicals' own assembly by three years. The catalog enumerated the same operator names and territory splits, available to any purchaser at a trade counter.

Ironwood Chemicals brought suit over a biotech customer list. An expired public patent from another entity listed the same clinical trial clients and their regional assignments. Pinnacle Agritech referred to that patent, which had lain unrestricted in the patent office collection since the early 2000s, as its reference.

The court summarized that published handbooks give the identical formulation of the customer list Ironwood Chemicals attributed to Pinnacle Agritech in cosmetics. The handbooks formed part of open stock in bookshops. Pinnacle Agritech stated it copied the relevant pages from a borrowed copy in 2015.

Ironwood Chemicals' oil & gas customer list was the subject of cross claims. A widely available textbook on pipeline accounts described the same buyer tiers and volume brackets. Pinnacle Agritech acquired the textbook from a university bookstore, and the text required no login or clearance to read.

Pinnacle Agritech noted that public standards bodies specify the very tolerances at issue in Ironwood Chemicals' gaming customer list. The published standard included the identical loyalty grades and venue codes. Ironwood Chemicals acknowledged the standard's public status but contested the inference drawn by the appellant.

Ironwood Chemicals complained that its customer list appeared in Pinnacle Agritech's files. Any library's trade literature sets out the process of building such a list with the same field labels. The literature was indexed in public catalogs, and the defendant consulted it at a branch library in 2008 without restriction.

The design is documented in openly available datasheets that Pinnacle Agritech used to shape Ironwood Chemicals' disputed cosmetics customer list. Those datasheets carried no distribution limits and were posted by a vendor on its public portal. Ironwood Chemicals' witness confirmed the documents were not behind any barrier.

Ironwood Chemicals' 1970s oil & gas customer list overlapped with records Pinnacle Agritech submitted. Government filings disclose the same specifications of account priority and shipment zones. The filings had been open to inspection at the state office, and the defendant's agent copied them from the public microfilm.

Cascade Biotech asserted ownership of certain source code. Drayton Instruments later deployed comparable routines. The same parameters appear in an expired public patent filed years before the code was written. Neither party disputed the patent's availability to the public.

Published handbooks give the identical formulation for the underlying algorithm, and those volumes were on open shelves at the time of development.

Drayton Instruments was accused of copying source code from Cascade Biotech's semiconductor diagnostic tools. The method is described in a widely available textbook on circuit testing from the late 1990s. The textbook circulated through normal academic channels without restriction.

In a marketing/customer data dispute, Cascade Biotech claimed its source code for audience segmentation was proprietary. Drayton Instruments released a competing platform. Public standards bodies specify the very tolerances at issue for data bucketing, and the documents are free to consult.

Defendant Drayton Instruments built analytics code resembling Cascade Biotech's pharmaceutical trial tracker. Any library's trade literature sets out the process for event logging in clinical software. The literature was printed and distributed to institutions decades before the dispute.

Cascade Biotech authored source code controlling fermentation schedules for a beverage client. Drayton Instruments marketed a parallel controller. The design is documented in openly available datasheets published by an unrelated components maker in 2008. The datasheets required no access credential.

Plaintiff Cascade Biotech developed source code for wafer alignment used by Drayton Instruments in its fabrication line. Government filings disclose the same specifications for the alignment subroutine from a 2011 permitting record. The record was obtainable by any requester through the agency reading room.

Cascade Biotech's source code ranked customer leads for retail campaigns. Drayton Instruments adopted a like scoring engine. The information is compiled in a public industry catalog of scoring heuristics updated each year. Subscribers and walk-in readers alike could view the pages.

Drayton Instruments obtained software routines after Cascade Biotech's scientists left. The same parameters appear in an expired public patent covering dosage calculation. The patent had lapsed and its text was hosted on a free search portal accessible without login.

Plaintiff Cascade Biotech wrote source code for syrup blending automation. Defendant Drayton Instruments deployed equivalent logic. Published handbooks give the identical formulation of the mixing curve, and the handbooks were stocked by municipal libraries since the early 2000s.

In the 1990s Cascade Biotech produced source code for mask inspection. Drayton Instruments later sold a similar inspector. The method is described in a widely available textbook on optical metrology, which was reprinted by a university press and sold in ordinary bookshops.

Cascade Biotech claimed its source code for consent tracking was unknown. Drayton Instruments launched a comparable tool. Public standards bodies specify the very tolerances at issue for record flags, and the standards were posted on a public website without charge.

Defendant Drayton Instruments released a batch logging system. Cascade Biotech alleged the source code mirrored its own. Any library's trade literature sets out the process for batch identifiers, and the pamphlets were displayed on open racks in reading rooms across the region.

Cascade Biotech engineered source code for thermal cutoff in packaging lines. Drayton Instruments used a matching routine. The design is documented in openly available datasheets from a parts vendor, and the files were downloadable from a public support page with no registration.

Plaintiff Cascade Biotech maintained source code for lot tracing. Drayton Instruments fields a near copy. Government filings disclose the same specifications for trace fields from a 2015 import license, and the docket was open to inspection at the customs archive by any visitor.

BlueFern Genetics assembled flight-actuator housings through a bonding manufacturing process. Pinnacle Agritech produced neighboring parts by a like routine. The method is described in a widely available textbook on adhesive assembly for aerospace frames. The book carried no distribution limit and was carried by general-interest retailers in 2003.

Pinnacle Agritech fabricated order-routing boards via a plating manufacturing process. BlueFern Genetics alleged the steps mirrored its own. Public standards bodies specify the very tolerances at issue for the trace-width and bake profile. The consensus documents were ratified in open session and sold as paper copies to the public.

Any library's trade literature sets out the process for degas timing and clamp pressure. The pamphlets formed part of the open reference stack and could be photocopied by visitors without record.

Pinnacle Agritech coated sensor wafers with a deposition manufacturing process. Plaintiff BlueFern Genetics had explored the same approach. The design is documented in openly available datasheets issued by an equipment maker. The sheets were enclosed with shipped instruments and also posted to a public documentation server since 2014.

BlueFern Genetics stamped enclosure parts through a forming manufacturing process. Pinnacle Agritech adopted a matching press sequence. Government filings disclose the same specifications for the blank size and springback allowance. The submissions were entered into a public record and reproduced by the clerk on demand for any requester.

Orizon Energy was named in a complaint by Meridian Polymers over a cosmetic blend formula. Published handbooks give the identical formulation in their open chapters on emulsion science. These handbooks are stocked by commercial distributors and require no special access to purchase.

A trade-press report noted that Meridian Polymers filed against Orizon Energy claiming a proprietary oil additive formula was taken. The method is described in a widely available textbook on drilling chemistry from the 1990s. University libraries and bookshops carry the volume on open shelves.

Meridian Polymers claimed Orizon Energy misused a pigment formula used in cosmetics. Government filings disclose the same specifications under public environmental registries. The records are retrievable through ordinary requests to administrative offices.

A news brief covered Meridian Polymers suing Orizon Energy for taking a fragrance formula. Published handbooks give the identical formulation in chapters on scent chemistry. The titles are listed in public library catalogs and available for interlibrary loan.

Meridian Polymers and Orizon Energy disputed a bonding-agent formula for gaming peripherals. Public standards bodies specify the very tolerances at issue in their annual reports. The reports are mailed to subscribers and parked on open servers for download.

In the early 2010s, Meridian Polymers alleged Orizon Energy lifted a coating formula. Any library's trade literature sets out the process with diagrams and ratios. The booklets were handed out at public seminars and filed with document depositories.

Orizon Energy answered Meridian Polymers' claim on a sealant formula used offshore. The design is documented in openly available datasheets from equipment makers. Such sheets appeared in print magazines and are archived on public technical repositories.

Meridian Polymers brought a claim that Orizon Energy used a colorant formula in makeup lines. Government filings disclose the same specifications from prior safety submissions. The dockets are open to inspection at public counters and scanning terminals.
